docs.title: Welcome to TechAlliance Knowledge Hub
docs.text:
TechAlliance is Southwestern Ontario's Regional Innovation Centre. We support ambitious founders, technology startups, and scaling companies by connecting them with the expertise, relationships, and opportunities they need to build stronger businesses.

Our mission is to champion, coach, and amplify businesses while creating a vibrant technology community.

We work alongside entrepreneurs at every stage of growth, helping them navigate challenges, make informed decisions, and discover new opportunities.

docs.title: How we help you move forward
docs.text:
• Access practical guidance: Gain perspective from experienced advisors who understand the challenges of building and growing a business.
  • Build meaningful connections: Connect with founders, industry experts, partners, and members of the technology community.
  • Explore growth opportunities: Discover relevant initiatives, relationships, and opportunities that support your business goals.
  • Grow with your community: Learn from other entrepreneurs, share experiences, and build relationships that support long-term success.

docs.title: Knowledge to support your next step
docs.text:
The TechAlliance knowledge hub brings together technical knowledge and resources to help you explore important topics, build your understanding, and make more informed decisions as your business grows.

Explore the resources available to you, find information relevant to your current challenges, and take your next step with greater clarity.

Ready to move forward?

Explore the knowledge hub or connect with TechAlliance to discover how our community can support your business.

docs.title: Getting started with the TechAlliance Knowledge Hub
docs.text:
Welcome to the TechAlliance Knowledge Hub.

Building and growing a technology business involves learning, testing ideas, and making important decisions along the way.

This hub brings together practical knowledge, tools, and resources to help you explore business concepts, work through challenges, and make informed decisions as your business develops.

You can explore the content on your own or follow the resources recommended by your TechAlliance advisor.

docs.title: 1. Start with your advisor's recommendations
docs.text:
Your TechAlliance advisor may share links to specific topics or resources based on your business goals and current challenges.

Start with the resources your advisor recommends. They're intended to help you focus on what's most relevant to your business right now.

You don't need to complete every section or follow a specific order. The hub is designed to support your learning whenever you need it.

docs.title: 2. Explore the topics relevant to your business
docs.text:
The hub organizes resources around five stages of business development:

  • Idea: Bring your idea to paper, research the opportunity, and explore the problem you want to solve.
  • Discovery: Move beyond initial research to investigate and validate the problem through conversations, observations, and evidence.
  • Validation: Test your proposed solution, gather customer feedback, and evaluate whether it addresses the problem you've identified.
  • Efficiency: Build the business foundations, processes, and systems needed to operate effectively.
  • Scale: Explore opportunities to grow your business, reach new markets, and manage the challenges of expansion.

Select a stage from the navigation menu to explore its available topics.

These stages provide a way to organize knowledge, not a fixed path that every business must follow.

You may find useful resources across several stages, regardless of where your business is today.

docs.title: 3. Explore the resources and put them to use
docs.text:
Each topic may include practical notes, useful tools, templates, or links to additional reading from external sources.

As you explore the resources:

  1. Understand: Review the information provided to become familiar with the topic and its key concepts.
  2. Explore: Check out the recommended tools, templates, and additional resources that can help you learn more.
  3. Apply: Consider how the information relates to your business and use what is relevant to your current challenges.
  4. Take notes: Keep track of useful insights, questions, and ideas to discuss with your TechAlliance advisor.

You don't need to use every resource or explore every external link. Focus on what helps you better understand the topic and make progress toward your business goals.

docs.title: 4. Find what you need
docs.text:
Looking for something specific?

Use the search bar to find topics related to your current questions or challenges.

You can also browse the navigation menu to explore resources organized by stage.

If you're unsure where to start, consider the most important question or challenge your business is facing right now.

docs.title: 5. Discuss your progress with your advisor
docs.text:
As you explore the resources, keep track of what you've learned, what you've applied, and where you need more guidance.

Consider bringing these questions to your next conversation:

  • What did I learn that could help my business?
  • What ideas or assumptions should I explore further?
  • What tools or resources could I put into practice?
  • What questions or challenges remain?
  • What should I focus on next?

Your TechAlliance advisor can help you reflect on your findings, identify relevant opportunities, and consider your next steps.

docs.title: Make the most of your learning
docs.text:
Focus on what's relevant. You don't need to read the entire hub. Start with the topics that address your current needs.

Learn at your own pace. Some topics may require more time or research. Return to resources whenever you need them.

Put knowledge into practice. Look for opportunities to apply what you've learned to real decisions and challenges in your business.

Ask questions. If something isn't clear, make a note and discuss it with your TechAlliance advisor.

Revisit topics as your business evolves. New challenges may bring you back to earlier stages or introduce topics you haven't explored yet.

docs.title: Ready to get started?
docs.text:
Open the first resource recommended by your TechAlliance advisor, or explore the topics available in the navigation menu.

Start with what matters most to your business right now, and use the knowledge you gain to take your next step.

docs.title: Understand your customers and explore the opportunity
docs.text:
You have an idea worth exploring. Now it's time to learn more about the people you're hoping to serve, the challenges they face, and how your proposed solution might fit into their lives or businesses.

The Discovery stage helps you move beyond assumptions by gathering insights, understanding customer needs, and exploring the market opportunity in greater detail.

You don't need to have a finished product or all the answers. This is your opportunity to listen, ask questions, and use what you learn to shape your next steps.

docs.title: What you'll explore
docs.text:
The resources in this section can help you:

  • Understand your customers: Learn more about your potential customers, their needs, behaviours, and priorities.
  • Explore customer problems: Investigate the challenges people experience and how they currently address them.
  • Conduct customer discovery: Learn how to approach conversations, ask useful questions, and gather meaningful feedback.
  • Assess the market opportunity: Explore market demand, existing alternatives, and potential opportunities for your idea.
  • Refine your assumptions: Use what you learn to revisit your initial thinking and identify areas that need further investigation.

docs.title: How to use these resources
docs.text:
Explore the topics available in this section to build a deeper understanding of your potential customers and the opportunity you're considering.

Each topic may include practical notes, tools, templates, or links to additional reading that can help you plan your research, gather insights, and organize your findings.

If your TechAlliance advisor has recommended specific resources, start there. You can return to other topics as your questions and priorities evolve.

docs.title: Questions to consider
docs.text:
As you explore your opportunity, think about:

  • Who are my potential customers, and what matters most to them?
  • What challenges are they experiencing?
  • How are they currently solving these problems?
  • What have I learned from speaking with potential customers?
  • What assumptions have been supported or challenged by my research?
  • What do I still need to understand before testing my proposed solution?

Use these questions to guide your research, reflect on your findings, and prepare for conversations with your TechAlliance advisor.

docs.title: Your next step
docs.text:
Start with the topic that helps you better understand your customers or address an important question about your opportunity.

Use what you learn to refine your understanding of the problem, identify potential opportunities, and prepare to test your assumptions in the Validation stage.

docs.title: Understand your customers before building your solution
docs.text:
You've researched your market, explored potential customer segments, and identified a problem your business might solve.

Now it's time to find out whether that problem exists in the lives of real people.

Customer discovery is the process of learning directly from potential customers about their experiences, challenges, behaviours, and needs.

It often involves one-on-one interviews where you ask people to describe how they handle a particular situation, what difficulties they experience, and what they've already done to address them.

The goal is to move beyond assumptions and understand the problem from the customer's perspective.

At this stage, you're not trying to convince people to buy your product or approve your idea. You're trying to learn whether the problem is real, who experiences it, and how important it is to them.

Customer discovery is about validating the problem, not selling the solution.

docs.title: Why customer discovery matters
docs.text:
Market research can help you identify trends, potential customer groups, and opportunities. But it doesn't always explain how people experience a problem in their daily lives.

Speaking directly with potential customers can help you understand:

  • The problem: What challenges do people actually experience?
  • The context: When, where, and why does the problem occur?
  • The impact: How much time, money, effort, or frustration does it create?
  • Current alternatives: How are people addressing the problem today?
  • Customer priorities: Is solving the problem important enough for them to take action?
  • Customer segments: Which groups appear to experience the problem most frequently or intensely?

You may discover that your original assumptions were correct, partially correct, or completely different from what customers experience.

All of these outcomes provide useful information.

Learning that a problem isn't important to your intended customers can help you reconsider your approach before investing significant time and resources into building a solution.

docs.title: Talk about experiences, not hypothetical situations
docs.text:
One of the most important principles of customer discovery is to focus on what people have actually experienced.

For example, asking someone, "Would you use an app that makes scheduling easier?" may lead to an encouraging answer.

But that answer doesn't tell you whether scheduling is a significant problem, how often it occurs, or whether the person would change their current approach.

Instead, ask questions such as:

  • "Can you tell me about the last time you had difficulty scheduling something?"
  • "What happened?"
  • "How did you handle it?"
  • "What made that situation difficult?"
  • "Have you tried anything to make the process easier?"

These questions encourage people to share specific experiences rather than speculate about what they might do in the future.

What customers have done is generally more useful evidence than what they say they might do.

docs.title: Who should you interview?
docs.text:
Start with people who match the potential customer segments you've identified.

For example, if your proposed solution addresses a problem experienced by restaurant managers, prioritize conversations with people who manage restaurants or regularly perform the relevant work.

Avoid relying only on friends, family members, or people who already support your idea. Their feedback may be influenced by their relationship with you.

Consider reaching potential interview participants through:

  • Professional networks and industry associations
  • LinkedIn and relevant online communities
  • Local business and community events
  • Introductions from existing contacts
  • Organizations serving your target customer segment

When reaching out, explain that you're researching a problem and would value their experience.

Make it clear that you're not contacting them to sell something.

For B2B businesses, remember that the person experiencing the problem may not be the person responsible for purchasing a solution.

You may eventually need to understand the perspectives of users, managers, and decision-makers.

docs.title: How to conduct a customer discovery interview
docs.text: You don't need a complicated process to get started. A focused conversation with a clear learning objective can provide valuable insights.

docs.title: 1. Define what you want to learn
docs.text:
Before the interview, identify the assumptions you're trying to investigate.

For example:

"We believe independent retailers regularly struggle with managing inventory across multiple sales channels."

Your interview should help you understand whether that challenge exists, how it affects retailers, and what they're currently doing about it.

docs.title: 2. Prepare open-ended questions
docs.text:
Create a short interview guide focused on the customer's experiences.

Use it to keep the conversation on track, but don't treat it as a script you must follow exactly.

Be prepared to ask follow-up questions when someone shares an interesting experience.

docs.title: 3. Explain the purpose of the conversation
docs.text:
Introduce yourself and explain that you're learning about how people experience a particular challenge.

Let the participant know there are no right or wrong answers.

If you'd like to record the conversation, ask for permission first and explain how the recording will be used and stored.

docs.title: 4. Listen more than you speak
docs.text:
Give the participant time to explain their experiences.

Avoid interrupting, suggesting answers, or immediately introducing your proposed solution.

When they describe a problem, ask for a specific example.

Questions such as "What happened next?" or "Can you tell me more about that?" can help you understand the situation in greater detail.

docs.title: 5. Explore the impact and current alternatives
docs.text:
Try to understand what the problem costs the customer in time, money, effort, or missed opportunities.

Ask what they've already tried and why their current approach may or may not be working.

docs.title: 6. Close and document what you learned
docs.text:
Before ending, ask whether there's anything important you haven't covered.

You can also ask whether the participant knows someone else who might be willing to share their experience.

After the conversation, review your notes while the details are still fresh.

Record what the person actually said or described, and distinguish those observations from your own interpretations.

docs.title: Customer discovery interview guide
docs.text:
Use the following questions as a starting point for your interviews.

Adapt them to the problem you're investigating and the customer segment you're speaking with.

Understanding the customer

  • Can you tell me a little about your role or daily activities?
  • How do you currently handle [RELEVANT ACTIVITY OR PROCESS]?
  • What tools or methods do you use?

Exploring the problem

  • What's the most challenging part of that process?
  • Can you tell me about the last time you experienced that challenge?
  • What happened?
  • How often does something like that occur?
  • What makes it difficult?

Understanding the impact

  • How does this challenge affect your work or daily life?
  • How much time or effort does it typically require?
  • What happens when the problem isn't resolved?
  • Who else is affected?

Exploring current alternatives

  • What have you tried to address the problem?
  • How are you handling it today?
  • What works well about your current approach?
  • What doesn't work as well?
  • Have you spent money or resources trying to improve the situation?

Closing the conversation

  • Is there anything important about this experience that I haven't asked?
  • Is there someone else you think I should speak with?
  • Would you be comfortable if I contacted you with additional questions?

You don't need to ask every question in every interview.

Focus on understanding the participant's experiences and follow up when their answers reveal something important.

docs.title: Customer discovery notes template
docs.text:
Use a consistent format to document what you learn from each conversation.

Category Notes Interview date Customer segment Participant role or context Main problem described Specific example shared Frequency of the problem Impact on the customer Current solution or workaround Previous attempts to solve it Important observations Assumptions supported or challenged Questions to investigate further

Avoid collecting unnecessary personal information.

If you record or transcribe interviews, obtain appropriate consent and store the information securely.

docs.title: Problem validation matrix
docs.text:
After conducting several interviews, compare your findings to identify patterns.

Create a table that summarizes the problems mentioned by different participants.

Problem Participants who mentioned it Reported impact Current alternatives Evidence or examples Problem A Problem B Problem C

Look for:

  • Problems mentioned repeatedly
  • Similar experiences across participants
  • Evidence of time, money, or effort already spent
  • Workarounds people have developed
  • Differences between customer segments
  • Findings that challenge your original assumptions

Don't assume a problem is important simply because several people mention it.

Consider its frequency, severity, consequences, and whether customers are already taking action to address it.

docs.title: Interview synthesis
docs.text:
Once you've collected several interviews, summarize what you've learned.

Try organizing your findings into four categories:

  1. Customer problems: What difficulties are people experiencing?
  2. Current behaviours: How are they addressing those difficulties?
  3. Problem impact: What consequences do those difficulties create?
  4. Unanswered questions: What do you still need to investigate?

Use the summary to refine your understanding of the customer segment and the problem.

If the findings are inconsistent, you may need to speak with more people or reconsider whether you're interviewing the right customer group.

docs.title: Google Forms
docs.text:
Google Forms can help you collect basic information from potential interview participants before scheduling a conversation.

For example, you can use a short form to confirm whether someone fits the customer segment you're researching.

Forms can also help organize contact preferences and scheduling information.

Keep the form brief. A questionnaire shouldn't replace the deeper conversations needed for customer discovery.

docs.title: Calendly
docs.text:
Calendly is a scheduling platform that can help you arrange interviews without exchanging multiple emails.

You can share your availability and allow participants to choose a suitable meeting time.

This can be useful when coordinating interviews with people outside your organization.

docs.title: Google Meet
docs.text:
Google Meet is a video meeting platform you can use to conduct remote customer discovery interviews.

Remote conversations can help you reach potential customers outside your immediate geographic area.

If you plan to record a meeting, confirm that the feature is available in your account and obtain the participant's permission.

docs.title: Google Sheets
docs.text:
Google Sheets can help you organize interview notes, compare findings, and identify recurring themes.

Create a spreadsheet using the customer discovery notes template or problem validation matrix.

Keep interview records organized and limit access to people who need the information.

docs.title: ChatGPT / Claude / DeepSeek / Augure[1]
docs.text:
These can help you review an interview guide for leading questions, organize anonymized notes, and identify potential themes across interviews.

They can also help you prepare neutral follow-up questions.

However, AI-generated summaries may overlook important details or misinterpret what participants said.

Review the original notes or transcripts before drawing conclusions.

AI-generated customer personas or simulated interviews are not substitutes for conversations with real potential customers.

Avoid sharing identifiable participant information, confidential business details, or interview recordings with AI tools without appropriate consent and safeguards.

[1]: Augure is the only fully Canadian option from this list

docs.title: Curo - Master customer discovery interviews for your startup
Kromatic - Customer discovery interviews: A founder's how-to guide
Put it into practice
docs.text:
Conduct your first round of customer discovery interviews.

Start by selecting one potential customer segment and one problem you want to investigate.

Write down your current assumptions:

  • Who experiences the problem?
  • When does the problem occur?
  • Why do you believe it's important?
  • How do you think customers currently address it?

Next, prepare a short interview guide using the questions provided on this page.

Aim to speak with at least five people who fit your target customer segment as an initial round of discovery.

This is a starting point, not a fixed requirement for validating a problem. You may need additional interviews as you learn more.

For each conversation:

  1. Prepare: Confirm that the participant fits your target segment and identify what you want to learn.
  2. Listen: Ask about real experiences and avoid pitching your proposed solution.
  3. Document: Record the problems, behaviours, workarounds, and consequences described.
  4. Compare: Look for similarities and differences across interviews.
  5. Reflect: Identify which assumptions were supported, challenged, or left unanswered.

Once you've completed your initial interviews, summarize your findings.

Ask yourself:

  • Did participants describe the problem without needing me to suggest it?
  • Can they recall specific situations when it occurred?
  • How frequently or seriously does the problem affect them?
  • Are they already spending time, money, or effort addressing it?
  • Did similar patterns appear across multiple interviews?
  • What surprised me or contradicted my assumptions?
  • Do I need to investigate a different customer segment or problem?

Don't worry if your findings challenge your original idea.

The purpose of customer discovery is to learn what matters to potential customers, not to prove that your first assumption was correct.

Consider reviewing your interview findings with your TechAlliance advisor to decide what to investigate next.

As you build confidence that a meaningful problem exists, you'll be better prepared to explore and eventually validate a solution.

docs.title: Plan how your business will reach its first customers
docs.text:
You've researched your market, explored your competition, identified potential customer segments, and spoken directly with people experiencing the problem you want to solve.

Now it's time to start thinking about how your business could reach those customers.

A go-to-market (GTM) strategy is a plan for introducing a product or service to a target market, reaching potential customers, communicating its value, and generating sales.

It connects what you're building with the people who may benefit from it.

Your go-to-market strategy can help you answer questions such as:

  • Who should we focus on reaching first?
  • Where and how can we connect with those customers?
  • What problem should our messaging emphasize?
  • How will customers learn about, evaluate, and purchase our solution?
  • Which sales, marketing, and partnership activities are worth exploring?
  • What resources will we need?
  • How will we measure whether our approach is working?

At the Discovery stage, you're creating an initial GTM draft, not a final launch plan.

Your understanding of the market has improved, but you may not have validated your proposed solution or demonstrated that customers are willing to pay for it.

The purpose of this exercise is to organize your assumptions, identify promising approaches, and prepare for the experiments you'll conduct as your business develops.

A good GTM draft gives you direction without committing you to a strategy that hasn't been tested.

docs.title: Build your plan around your customer research
docs.text:
Your GTM strategy should begin with what you've learned about your potential customers.

Review the findings from your:

  • Competition analysis
  • Potential customer segments research
  • Customer discovery interviews
  • Subject-matter expert interviews
  • Product roadmap

Together, these resources can help you understand who your customers might be, what matters to them, and how they currently discover and evaluate solutions.

For example, if you're developing software for small manufacturers, your research might suggest that potential customers rely on industry associations, professional referrals, or trade events when evaluating new technology.

Those insights could make partnerships and direct outreach more promising starting points than broad consumer advertising.

However, these are still assumptions until you've tested them.

Prioritize channels based on evidence about customer behaviour, not simply because they're popular.

docs.title: Identify your initial target market
docs.text:
Trying to reach everyone at once can make your marketing and sales efforts expensive and difficult to manage.

Start by choosing a specific customer segment.

Consider:

  • Who experiences the problem most frequently or intensely?
  • Who is already investing time or money in addressing it?
  • Which customers can you realistically reach?
  • Who is involved in the purchasing decision?
  • Where are those customers located?
  • Are there industry, geographic, or regulatory factors that affect your approach?

For B2B businesses, distinguish between the person who uses the solution and the person who approves or pays for it.

For B2C businesses, consider the customer's needs, purchasing habits, and the situations that might motivate them to act.

Your initial target market doesn't need to be your only market forever.

It should give you a focused starting point for learning what works.

docs.title: Understand how customers discover and buy solutions
docs.text:
A customer rarely moves directly from hearing about a business to making a purchase.

They may first recognize a problem, search for information, compare alternatives, speak with colleagues, request a demonstration, or seek approval from someone else.

This process is often called the customer journey or buying journey.

Understanding it can help you identify the activities and channels that deserve attention.

Consider the following stages:

Awareness

How do potential customers recognize the problem and discover possible solutions?

Examples might include online searches, professional networks, social media, referrals, and industry events.

Consideration

How do customers compare different approaches?

They may review websites, read case studies, ask peers for recommendations, or speak with vendors.

Decision

What needs to happen before they commit?

Depending on the business, this could involve a purchase, trial, demonstration, proposal, procurement review, or internal approval.

Onboarding and retention

What will customers need after they begin using the solution?

Think about support, education, implementation, and the experience required to help them receive value.

You may not know every step yet.

Use your customer interviews to identify what you've learned and what still needs to be investigated.

docs.title: Explore distribution and acquisition channels
docs.text:
A distribution channel is how your product or service reaches customers.

A customer acquisition channel is how you attract and convert potential customers.

Sometimes these overlap, but they aren't always the same.

For example, a software company might attract customers through LinkedIn but deliver its product through its own website.

Potential channels include:

Channel How it might be used Direct sales Reach potential customers through personalized conversations and outreach Website and search Help customers discover and evaluate your offering online Social media Build awareness, share useful information, and connect with relevant communities Email marketing Maintain relationships with people who have agreed to receive communications Industry events Meet potential customers, partners, and industry professionals Referral networks Reach new customers through trusted introductions Strategic partnerships Work with organizations that already serve your target audience Marketplaces and platforms Make products or services available through established platforms Retail or distributors Reach customers through physical stores, resellers, or distribution partners Paid advertising Test targeted messages and reach potential customers through advertising platforms

Not every channel will make sense for your venture.

Consider where your target customers spend their time, how they make purchasing decisions, and what it would cost to reach them.

At this stage, selecting one or two promising channels to investigate is often more useful than trying to establish a presence everywhere.

docs.title: Plan your sales and outreach approach
docs.text:
Your GTM draft should explain how you expect to start conversations with potential customers.

Depending on your business, this might involve:

  • Founder-led outreach to prospective customers
  • Introductions through professional networks
  • Relationships with industry associations
  • Participation in relevant events
  • Partnerships with complementary businesses
  • Inbound inquiries through your website
  • Targeted email or social outreach

For early-stage ventures, founder-led sales conversations can be especially useful because they provide direct feedback about customer needs, objections, and buying decisions.

Before investing in a large sales team or complex systems, learn whether your outreach approach generates meaningful conversations.

Consider:

  • Who should you contact?
  • Why would they be interested in speaking with you?
  • What value can you offer during the conversation?
  • What action are you asking them to take?
  • How will you track responses and follow-ups?

Remember that contacting potential customers for research is different from selling to them.

Be transparent about the purpose of your outreach and follow applicable privacy and anti-spam requirements.

docs.title: Develop your initial marketing message
docs.text:
Your marketing message should connect the customer problem to the value your proposed solution aims to provide.

Start with what you learned during customer discovery.

Consider:

  • What problem does the customer recognize?
  • How do customers describe that problem in their own words?
  • Why does solving it matter?
  • What outcome would be valuable to them?
  • How might your proposed approach differ from existing alternatives?

Avoid making claims about results, capabilities, or customer satisfaction that you haven't demonstrated.

At the Discovery stage, your message is a hypothesis to test.

For example:

Problem-focused message:

"Preparing weekly reports shouldn't require hours of manual data collection."

Proposed value message:

"We're exploring a simpler way for small teams to bring their reporting information together."

The second example communicates a direction without claiming that the product already delivers a proven result.

As you validate your solution, you can make your messaging more specific and evidence-based.

docs.title: Keep your first GTM plan capital-efficient
docs.text:
Early-stage ventures often have limited time, money, and people available.

Your initial GTM approach should help you learn without requiring a large upfront investment.

Before committing resources, ask:

  • Can we test this channel on a small scale?
  • Can the founders manage the initial outreach?
  • What do we need to prepare before testing?
  • How much time and money would the test require?
  • What would indicate that the approach is promising?
  • What would cause us to change direction?

A small number of focused experiments can provide more useful information than a broad campaign with unclear objectives.

For example, you might compare personalized outreach to a small group of potential customers with introductions through an industry association.

The goal is to learn which approach generates relevant conversations, not simply which produces the most impressions or clicks.

docs.title: Customer Zoom Tool
docs.text:
The Customer Zoom Tool, developed by Moves the Needle, helps you identify specific potential customers rather than relying only on broad market segments or general customer personas.

Instead of starting with categories such as age, industry, or company size, the tool encourages you to focus on the traits and observable behaviours that distinguish people who experience the problem you're trying to solve.

Using insights from your customer discovery interviews, work through three steps:

  1. Identify distinctive traits: Think about one person you've interviewed and list at least 10 characteristics that make them relevant to your proposed solution. Select the three most distinctive traits.
  2. Identify observable behaviours: List at least 10 actions or habits that could help you recognize someone experiencing the problem. Select the three most distinctive behaviours.
  3. Describe a specific customer: Use those traits and behaviours to describe a real person who represents the type of customer you want to reach.

Repeat the exercise with other interview participants to explore whether different customer groups share similar problems, traits, and behaviours.

If your business serves multiple customer groups, such as buyers and end users, consider completing a separate exercise for each.

How does this help your GTM strategy?

A more specific understanding of your customer can help you decide:

  • Where to find people who match your target customer profile
  • Which communities, networks, or organizations they participate in
  • What behaviours might indicate they're experiencing the problem
  • How to make your outreach and messaging more relevant
  • Which customer groups to prioritize during your initial GTM experiments

Remember that the tool should be grounded in real customer interviews, not an imaginary ideal customer.

The goal isn't to create a perfect persona. It's to identify recognizable people whose needs and behaviours can guide your next steps.

docs.title: Go-to-market planning canvas
docs.text:
Use a simple planning canvas to bring the main elements of your strategy together.

GTM element Questions to answer Target customer Who are we trying to reach first? Customer problem What important problem are we addressing? Proposed value What outcome do we hope to help customers achieve? Competition What alternatives are customers using today? Positioning Why might customers consider our approach? Distribution How will customers access our product or service? Acquisition channels How will potential customers discover us? Sales approach How will we start and manage customer conversations? Marketing activities What content, messages, or materials might we need? Partnerships Which organizations could help us reach customers? Resources What people, tools, time, and budget are available? Metrics How will we evaluate our initial experiments? Assumptions What still needs to be tested?

You don't need a perfect answer for every category.

The canvas should help you see which decisions are supported by research and which require further investigation.

docs.title: Channel prioritization matrix
docs.text:
Compare potential acquisition and distribution channels before deciding where to focus.

Channel Customer relevance Cost and effort Evidence Next experiment Direct outreach Industry partnerships Search and website Social media Events

For each channel, consider:

  • Do our target customers actually use this channel?
  • Can we reach the right people through it?
  • What would it cost to test?
  • What resources or partners would we need?
  • What evidence supports our assumptions?
  • What would we learn from a small experiment?

Select one or two channels for your initial testing plan.

Avoid treating a channel as proven simply because competitors use it.

docs.title: Six-week GTM planning framework
docs.text:
A six-week plan can help you organize your preparation and early experiments into manageable activities.

At the Discovery stage, treat this as a planning baseline. Activities that involve selling or promoting an unvalidated solution may need to wait until the Validation stage.

Week Focus Suggested activities 1 Review research Consolidate customer insights, competition findings, and assumptions 2 Define your approach Select an initial segment, draft positioning, and identify promising channels 3 Prepare materials Develop outreach messages, a basic value proposition, and any materials needed for research 4 Test channel assumptions Explore selected channels through conversations, introductions, or small-scale experiments 5 Review early signals Compare responses, objections, customer relevance, and effort required 6 Refine the plan Update priorities, identify remaining assumptions, and prepare the next round of validation

Your plan should reflect your actual resources and readiness.

You may need more time to investigate a market, secure introductions, or validate your proposed solution before conducting commercial experiments.

docs.title: GTM metrics and learning tracker
docs.text:
Metrics help you evaluate whether your activities are producing useful results.

For early-stage businesses, focus on a manageable number of indicators.

Potential metrics include:

  • Outreach response rate: The percentage of contacted prospects who respond.
  • Qualified conversations: The number of conversations with people who match your target customer profile.
  • Meeting conversion rate: The percentage of relevant outreach attempts that result in meetings.
  • Channel cost: The time and money required to test a particular channel.
  • Website conversion rate: The percentage of visitors who complete a defined action, when a website experiment is relevant.
  • Customer acquisition cost (CAC): The cost of acquiring a paying customer, once you have enough actual acquisition data to calculate it meaningfully.
  • Sales cycle length: The time between an initial sales opportunity and a completed purchase, once sales activity begins.
  • Customer feedback: The recurring questions, concerns, and objections you hear during conversations.

Not all of these metrics will be relevant or measurable during Discovery.

Start by tracking the activities you can actually perform and the signals that help you make decisions.

Be cautious about applying general industry benchmarks. Results can vary significantly by market, channel, product, price, and customer segment.

Where reliable benchmarks are unavailable, establish your own baseline through initial experiments.

docs.title: ChatGPT / Claude / DeepSeek / Augure[1]
docs.text:
They can help you organize market research, compare potential GTM channels, draft outreach messages, and create an initial project plan.

You can also use them to challenge assumptions and identify questions that need further research.

AI-generated recommendations should be treated as hypotheses until they're supported by credible sources or real customer evidence.

Use the following prompt as a starting point for researching your initial GTM strategy.

[1]: Augure is the only fully Canadian option from this list

Suggested AI prompt:

Act as an experienced Business Development Strategist with expertise in startup go-to-market planning, customer acquisition, distribution channels, market research, and capital-efficient growth.

I am developing a venture and need an evidence-based, practical six-week go-to-market planning baseline.

VENTURE INFORMATION

Venture name: [VENTURE NAME]
Website: [VENTURE WEBSITE URL, IF AVAILABLE]
Products or services: [DESCRIPTION OF PRODUCTS OR SERVICES]
Headquarters: [CITY, PROVINCE, COUNTRY]
Initial target geography: [TARGET MARKET OR REGION]
Business model: [B2B, B2C, B2B2C, OR OTHER]
Development stage: [DISCOVERY / VALIDATION / READY TO LAUNCH]
Available team and roles: [TEAM INFORMATION]
Estimated GTM budget: [BUDGET OR UNKNOWN]
Current product readiness: [WHAT EXISTS TODAY]

COMPETITIVE LANDSCAPE

[INSERT SUMMARY FROM COMPETITION ANALYSIS]

POTENTIAL CUSTOMER SEGMENTS

[INSERT SUMMARY FROM CUSTOMER SEGMENT RESEARCH]

CUSTOMER DISCOVERY FINDINGS

[INSERT SUMMARY OF INTERVIEWS, CUSTOMER PROBLEMS, CURRENT ALTERNATIVES, AND BUYING BEHAVIOURS]

SUBJECT-MATTER EXPERT INSIGHTS

[INSERT RELEVANT FINDINGS, IF AVAILABLE]

PRODUCT ROADMAP

[INSERT INITIAL PRIORITIES AND DESIRED CUSTOMER OUTCOMES]

YOUR TASK

Research relevant good practices, market evidence, and customer acquisition approaches to develop an initial six-week GTM plan.

Prioritize recommendations that are realistic for our development stage, target market, team capacity, and available budget.

Address the following areas:

1. DISTRIBUTION AND ACQUISITION CHANNELS

- Identify the most promising distribution and customer acquisition channels.
- Explain why each channel may fit our customer segment and buying behaviour.
- Distinguish how customers discover the offering from how they access or purchase it.
- Identify the preparation, resources, and potential partners required.
- Compare expected cost, effort, and uncertainty.
- Recommend one or two channels to investigate first.

2. SALES AND BUSINESS DEVELOPMENT

- Recommend a capital-efficient approach to initial outreach.
- Evaluate founder-led sales, events, industry associations, partnerships, referrals, and other relevant approaches.
- Explain whether hiring sales development representatives (SDRs) would be justified at our current stage.
- Suggest simple systems for tracking contacts, conversations, follow-ups, and outcomes.
- Identify any important considerations for outreach compliance and privacy.

3. MARKETING AND PROMOTION

- Recommend the essential marketing materials and activities needed at our current stage.
- Evaluate the relevance of website content, search, social media, email, events, partnerships, and paid advertising.
- Identify which activities should be tested first, deferred, or avoided.
- Suggest messages based on customer problems and desired outcomes.
- Do not invent customer testimonials, proven results, traction, or product capabilities.

4. METRICS AND BENCHMARKS

- Recommend a small set of useful KPIs for our stage.
- Define each metric and explain how to calculate it.
- Identify credible benchmarks where available and relevant.
- Cite the source, date, geography, and business context of each benchmark.
- Do not invent benchmarks or imply that industry averages are guaranteed targets.
- If reliable benchmarks are unavailable, recommend how to establish our own baseline.

5. SIX-WEEK PROJECT PLAN

Create one consolidated timeline covering all recommended activities.

For each task, include:
- Week
- Objective
- Activity
- Suggested owner or role
- Dependencies
- Expected deliverable
- Estimated effort or cost, where supportable
- Success or learning indicator

Identify key milestones and decision points.

Separate activities appropriate for Discovery from commercial activities that should wait until the solution is sufficiently validated.

RESEARCH REQUIREMENTS

Use credible and relevant sources where available, including:
- Government and statistical sources such as Statistics Canada
- Industry research and reports
- Relevant business and startup publications
- Competitor websites and publicly available materials
- Customer reviews and community discussions
- Search and competitive intelligence tools

Provide links for important factual claims, market observations, and benchmarks.

Clearly distinguish:
- Verified facts
- Findings provided in the venture information
- Reasonable assumptions
- Recommendations that require testing

Do not invent market data, competitor performance, customer behaviour, costs, conversion rates, or source citations.

If you cannot access live internet research, say so explicitly and do not present unsupported claims as verified research.

If important information is missing, state the assumptions used and explain how they affect the recommendations.

FINAL OUTPUT

Provide:

A. Executive summary of the proposed GTM direction
B. Prioritized distribution and acquisition channels
C. Sales and business development approach
D. Marketing and promotion priorities
E. KPI definitions and supported benchmarks
F. One consolidated six-week project plan
G. Key assumptions, risks, and questions to validate
H. Sources and references

Keep the recommendations practical, specific, and proportionate to the venture's stage and resources.

Review the output carefully.

Check the cited sources, question unsupported assumptions, and adjust the recommendations to reflect what you've learned from real customers.

Don't treat the AI-generated plan as a final strategy or a substitute for testing your approach.

docs.title: Put it into practice
docs.text:
Create a first draft of your go-to-market strategy.

Your goal isn't to launch a full marketing and sales campaign. It's to develop a focused plan that you can test and improve as your solution becomes ready.

Start by gathering the research you've completed during the Idea and Discovery stages.

Then:

  1. Choose your initial customer segment. Review your customer discovery interviews and complete the Customer Zoom Tool to identify the distinctive traits and behaviours of the people you want to reach first. Use those findings to refine your target customer profile.
  2. Define the customer problem. Summarize the challenge you're addressing and the outcome customers want.
  3. Draft your value proposition. Explain the value your proposed solution aims to provide without making unverified claims.
  4. Identify possible channels. List the ways you might reach and serve your target customers.
  5. Prioritize. Select one or two channels based on customer relevance, available resources, and supporting evidence.
  6. Plan outreach and promotion. Identify the conversations, materials, partnerships, or experiments needed to investigate those channels.
  7. Choose metrics. Decide what information will help you evaluate your approach.
  8. Build a six-week plan. Organize your tasks, responsibilities, dependencies, and milestones into one timeline.

You can use the suggested AI prompt to help research your options and develop the initial plan.

Before considering your draft complete, ask yourself:

  • Can I explain why I've chosen this customer segment?
  • Do I have evidence that my target customers use the channels I'm considering?
  • Does my messaging reflect problems identified during customer discovery?
  • Am I clear about how customers might discover, evaluate, and purchase the solution?
  • Have I considered partnerships and referrals as well as direct marketing?
  • Is my plan realistic for my available team, time, and budget?
  • Have I separated verified findings from assumptions?
  • What can I test now, and what should wait until the solution is validated?
  • What would cause me to change my approach?

Your GTM draft should be a working document.

Review it as you test your solution, learn more about your customers, and gather evidence about which channels and messages are effective.

Consider discussing your draft with your TechAlliance advisor to review your assumptions, priorities, and proposed experiments.

The goal of Discovery is to develop an informed direction. The next stage is about testing whether your proposed solution and approach can deliver value to real customers.

docs.title: Understand your intellectual property and avoid potential risks
docs.text:
As you explore your business idea and begin planning a product or service, you'll make decisions about technology, branding, designs, content, and other information that may have intellectual property implications.

Intellectual property (IP) refers to creations of the mind that may be protected through legal rights, such as inventions, original creative works, designs, and trademarks.

An IP strategy is a plan for identifying, managing, protecting, and using intellectual property in ways that support your business goals.

At the Discovery stage, your priority isn't necessarily to register patents or trademarks immediately.

Instead, focus on understanding:

  • What intellectual property your business may be creating
  • What intellectual property belongs to other people or organizations
  • Whether existing IP rights could affect your proposed product or business
  • Who owns the work being created for your venture
  • What information you may need to protect before sharing it publicly
  • When you should seek professional advice about registration or other protection

Understanding existing IP rights is just as important as protecting your own.

Addressing these questions early can help you avoid costly changes and make more informed decisions as your product develops.

docs.title: Understand the different types of IP
docs.text:
Different types of intellectual property protect different aspects of a business.

Some common examples include:

  • Patents: Can protect qualifying inventions, including certain products, processes, and technological improvements. Examples include:
  • A new medical device that uses an innovative mechanism to monitor a patient's health.
  • A novel manufacturing process that reduces material waste.

  • A new battery technology that improves energy storage efficiency.

  • Trademarks: Help distinguish your goods or services from those of other businesses. They can include names, logos, and other identifying signs. Examples include:

  • A distinctive company name used to identify your business's products or services.
  • A recognizable logo displayed on your products, website, or packaging.

  • A unique product name used to distinguish your offering from competitors.

  • Copyright: Can protect original works such as software code, written content, illustrations, and other creative material. Examples include:

  • Original source code written for a software application.
  • Photographs, illustrations, or graphics created for your website.

  • Original training materials, instructional videos, or written guides.

  • Industrial designs: Can protect qualifying visual features of a finished product, such as its shape, configuration, or ornamentation. Examples include:

  • The distinctive exterior shape of a wearable technology device.
  • A unique decorative pattern applied to a consumer product.

  • The original visual design of a product's casing or enclosure.

  • Trade secrets: Can protect valuable confidential business information when appropriate measures are taken to keep it secret. Examples include:

  • A confidential manufacturing formula or production method.
  • A proprietary algorithm or internal process that provides a competitive advantage and is kept confidential.
  • A confidential customer pricing model or business strategy that isn't publicly available.

These protections work differently.

For example, copyright generally arises automatically when an eligible original work is created, while patent protection generally requires an application and examination process.

Trade secrets depend on maintaining confidentiality rather than registering the information.

An idea by itself isn't automatically protected simply because you thought of it first.

Understanding these distinctions can help you recognize which aspects of your business may need attention.

docs.title: Make sure you're not infringing on someone else's IP
docs.text:
Before investing significant resources into developing a product, choosing a brand name, or entering a market, investigate whether other businesses or individuals hold relevant intellectual property rights.

IP infringement occurs when someone uses protected intellectual property in a way that violates the rights of its owner.

Potential issues include:

  • Choosing a business or product name that conflicts with an existing trademark
  • Developing or commercializing technology covered by another party's enforceable patent
  • Using images, text, software, or other copyrighted material without the necessary permission or licence
  • Incorporating third-party software without following its licence conditions
  • Using confidential information obtained from a previous employer, partner, or other organization without authorization
  • Creating a product design that conflicts with existing industrial design rights

Finding a similar product or brand doesn't automatically mean you're infringing someone's rights.

Likewise, finding no obvious match doesn't guarantee that your proposed name, product, or technology is safe to use.

The relevant rights, jurisdictions, and circumstances matter.

Use early research to identify potential concerns, then seek qualified IP advice when the risks or business decisions justify it.

docs.title: Understand freedom to operate
docs.text:
Freedom to operate (FTO) refers to whether you can carry out specific business activities, such as making, using, or selling a product, without infringing relevant IP rights held by others.

This is particularly important for technology businesses developing new products or processes.

For example, you might independently develop an invention that you believe is original.

However, another company may already hold a patent covering certain aspects of the technology in a market you intend to serve.

Even if you obtain your own patent for an improvement, that doesn't automatically give you permission to use another party's protected invention.

A professional freedom-to-operate assessment may involve reviewing relevant patents, claims, jurisdictions, legal status, and the activities your business intends to undertake.

A basic online search is not the same as a legal freedom-to-operate assessment.

At the Discovery stage, your goal is to recognize potential issues early and determine whether more detailed investigation is needed.

docs.title: Consider ownership and confidentiality
docs.text:
As you work with co-founders, employees, contractors, researchers, and external partners, be clear about who owns the intellectual property being created.

Don't assume that paying someone to develop software, create a design, or contribute to a project automatically gives your company every relevant IP right.

Ownership can depend on the circumstances, applicable law, and the agreements in place.

Consider:

  • Who created the work or invention?
  • Was it developed before or after the venture was established?
  • Were third-party resources, technologies, or materials involved?
  • Are there employment, contractor, university, or partnership agreements that affect ownership?
  • Does the company have the rights it needs to use and commercialize the work?

Confidentiality is another important consideration.

Sharing technical details, inventions, or other sensitive information publicly may affect your ability to protect certain IP rights later.

Before publishing technical information, demonstrating an invention, or discussing sensitive details with external parties, consider whether confidentiality measures or professional advice are needed.

Patent disclosure rules vary between countries, so timing can matter if you intend to seek protection internationally.

docs.title: Build an IP strategy that grows with your business
docs.text:
You don't need a complex IP portfolio to begin thinking strategically about intellectual property.

Start by identifying the IP relevant to your business and the decisions that may affect it.

Your approach may include:

  • Researching existing trademarks, patents, and other relevant rights
  • Keeping records of your inventions and original work
  • Reviewing third-party software and content licences
  • Clarifying ownership with people contributing to your venture
  • Protecting confidential business information
  • Identifying inventions, names, or designs that may eventually need formal protection
  • Seeking professional guidance before making important disclosure, registration, or commercialization decisions

Your IP strategy should evolve alongside your business.

Some assets may become more valuable as you validate your solution and prepare to enter the market. Others may not justify the cost of formal registration.

The goal is to make informed decisions rather than pursuing protection simply because it's available.

docs.title: Initial IP inventory
docs.text:
An IP inventory helps you identify the intellectual property your business has created, uses, or may need to protect.

Start by listing relevant assets and recording what you know about them.

IP asset Type of IP Creator or owner Current status Questions or next steps Business name Trademark Product design Industrial design or other rights Software code Copyright and licences Technical invention Potential patent or trade secret Confidential process Potential trade secret

These are examples. The relevant IP rights will depend on the nature of the asset.

Include third-party materials your business relies on, but distinguish them from assets your company owns.

Use the inventory to identify ownership questions, potential conflicts, and areas where professional advice may be valuable.

docs.title: Preliminary IP search checklist
docs.text:
A preliminary IP search helps you identify existing rights that may be relevant to your business.

Depending on your product or service, consider:

  1. Business and product names: Search for identical or similar names and trademarks in the markets you intend to serve.
  2. Technology and inventions: Investigate relevant patent publications and existing technical approaches.
  3. Product appearance: Explore registered industrial designs where visual features may be important.
  4. Software and content: Review licences and permissions for third-party code, images, written material, and other creative works.
  5. Ownership and agreements: Check whether existing contracts or relationships affect your right to use or commercialize relevant work.

Document your search terms, sources, dates, and findings.

Remember that preliminary searches can miss relevant rights. They do not establish legal clearance or guarantee freedom to operate.

docs.title: IP risk assessment
docs.text:
Use a simple risk assessment to prioritize questions that may affect your business.

Potential issue Business impact What you know Next step Similar trademark exists Third-party technology may be protected Software licence requirements are unclear Ownership of contractor-created work is uncertain Invention may be disclosed publicly

For each issue, consider:

  • How could it affect your proposed product or business?
  • What evidence do you have?
  • What information is missing?
  • Could the issue affect an upcoming decision?
  • Should you consult a qualified IP professional before proceeding?

Focus first on issues that could significantly affect your ability to develop, use, or commercialize your solution.

docs.title: IP strategy planning
docs.text:
Use your inventory and risk assessment to outline your initial approach.

Consider three priorities:

1. Understand and respect existing IP

Identify relevant third-party rights and determine where further investigation may be needed.

2. Establish ownership and protect important information

Clarify ownership of your work, maintain appropriate records, and consider confidentiality requirements.

3. Plan future protection

Identify potential trademarks, inventions, designs, or other assets that may warrant formal protection as your business develops.

You don't need to resolve every question immediately.

Your initial strategy should identify the decisions that matter now and the steps you'll need to take as you move toward product validation and commercialization.

docs.title: WIPO Global Brand Database
docs.text:
The World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO) provides the Global Brand Database to help users search trademark information from participating national and international collections.

You can use it to explore existing brand names, logos, and other trademarks that may be relevant to your proposed business or product name.

Try searching for:

  • Your proposed business name
  • Your proposed product name
  • Similar spellings or variations
  • Relevant words associated with your brand

Review results carefully, including the jurisdictions and goods or services involved.

The database doesn't include every possible trademark right, and a search with no matching results doesn't guarantee that a name is available to use or register.

docs.title: Canadian Trademarks Database
docs.text:
The Canadian Intellectual Property Office (CIPO) provides a searchable database of Canadian trademark records.

You can use it to investigate trademarks that may be relevant to your proposed business name, product name, or branding in Canada.

Search for identical and similar marks, then review the available information about their status and associated goods or services.

Trademark rights may also exist outside the registered records shown in the database.

For important branding decisions, consider obtaining a professional trademark clearance assessment rather than relying only on your own search.

Put it into practice
docs.text:
Create an initial IP inventory and identify potential risks related to your business idea.

Start by listing the intellectual property your venture creates, uses, or may depend on.

Consider your business name, proposed product name, software, technical inventions, designs, written materials, and confidential information.

Then:

  1. Identify: List the IP assets relevant to your venture, including important third-party materials.
  2. Check ownership: Record who created each asset and whether your company has the rights it needs.
  3. Research: Use the WIPO Global Brand Database and Canadian Trademarks Database to conduct preliminary searches for your proposed names.
  4. Explore risks: Identify potential trademark conflicts, third-party technology concerns, licence requirements, or ownership questions.
  5. Consider confidentiality: Review whether any inventions or sensitive information could be affected by upcoming public disclosures.
  6. Prioritize: Decide which issues need further research or professional guidance before you continue developing or commercializing your solution.

You don't need to register anything as part of this exercise.

The goal is to develop a clearer understanding of your IP position and identify decisions that shouldn't be overlooked.

Before moving forward, ask yourself:

  • Do I understand which types of IP may be relevant to my business?
  • Have I investigated whether my proposed business or product name may conflict with existing rights?
  • Am I using any third-party code, content, technology, or designs that require permission or licence compliance?
  • Do I know who owns the work being created for my venture?
  • Could an upcoming presentation, demonstration, or publication affect future protection?
  • Are there potential freedom-to-operate concerns that need professional assessment?
  • Which assets might be worth protecting as the business develops?

Summarize your findings and identify the questions you need to resolve.

Consider reviewing your initial IP strategy with your TechAlliance advisor and seeking advice from a qualified IP lawyer, patent agent, or trademark agent where appropriate.

Remember: The purpose of this exercise is to identify and manage potential IP risks, not to provide legal clearance.

As you move toward the Validation stage, revisit your IP strategy before making important decisions about product development, public disclosure, branding, or commercialization.

docs.title: Turn customer insights into a clear direction for your product
docs.text:
You've spoken with potential customers, explored the problems they experience, and gathered insights from subject-matter experts.

Now it's time to organize what you've learned and decide what your product should focus on.

A product roadmap is a visual plan that communicates the direction of your product, the problems you want to address, and the priorities that will guide its development.

It helps you connect your research to the decisions you'll make as you explore, design, test, and eventually build your solution.

At the Discovery stage, your roadmap doesn't need to be a detailed development schedule or a list of features with fixed delivery dates.

Instead, it should help you answer three questions:

  • What problems are we trying to solve?
  • Which problems should we focus on first?
  • What do we still need to learn before deciding how to solve them?

Your initial roadmap is a working plan. It should evolve as you gather more evidence and develop a better understanding of your customers.

docs.title: Start with what you've learned
docs.text:
Your customer discovery interviews and subject-matter expert conversations should be the starting point for your roadmap.

Review your interview notes and identify recurring themes.

For example, potential customers might have described:

  • Tasks that take too much time
  • Processes that are difficult or confusing
  • Existing tools that don't meet their needs
  • Expensive or inefficient workarounds
  • Problems that affect their ability to complete important work

Subject-matter experts may have also identified technical limitations, industry requirements, or other considerations that could influence your approach.

Organize these findings into a list of customer problems, needs, and opportunities.

Focus on the underlying problem rather than immediately deciding which feature to build.

For example, a customer might say they need an automated reporting dashboard.

Before adding a dashboard to your roadmap, investigate what they're actually trying to accomplish.

Perhaps their real challenge is spending several hours every week collecting information from different systems.

Understanding that problem gives you more flexibility to explore possible solutions.

docs.title: Prioritize problems before features
docs.text:
You probably won't be able to address every customer problem at once.

A roadmap helps you decide where to focus your attention and resources.

When comparing opportunities, consider:

  • Customer impact: How significantly does the problem affect the people experiencing it?
  • Frequency: How often does the problem occur?
  • Evidence: What have you learned from customer interviews or other research?
  • Customer segment: Is the problem especially relevant to the group you want to serve first?
  • Current alternatives: How are customers addressing the problem today?
  • Feasibility: Are there technical, operational, financial, or regulatory considerations that may affect your ability to address it?
  • Business relevance: Does addressing the problem align with the business you're trying to build?

You don't need a complex scoring system.

Start by identifying which problems appear most important and which assumptions still need to be investigated.

Avoid treating one person's feature request as proof that a particular solution should become a priority.

docs.title: Think about outcomes, not just deliverables
docs.text:
Traditional product roadmaps often focus on features and delivery dates.

For an early-stage venture, this can create commitments before you've gathered enough evidence to know which solutions will work.

An outcome-based roadmap focuses on the improvements you want to create rather than only the things you plan to build.

For example:

Feature-focused approach:

"Build an automated reporting dashboard."

Outcome-focused approach:

"Help customers reduce the time they spend preparing weekly reports."

The outcome gives you a clearer understanding of what you're trying to achieve while leaving room to explore different solutions.

Later, during the Validation stage, you can test prototypes, minimum viable products (MVPs), or other approaches to determine which solutions deliver the desired results.

docs.title: Keep your roadmap flexible
docs.text:
A product roadmap should provide direction without preventing you from responding to new information.

You may discover that:

  • A problem is less important than you initially believed.
  • A different customer segment experiences the problem more intensely.
  • A proposed feature doesn't address the underlying need.
  • A technical or regulatory requirement changes your priorities.
  • A simpler solution could deliver the same outcome.

These discoveries may require you to change your roadmap.

That's part of the process.

A roadmap isn't a promise to build everything you've listed. It's a tool for making informed decisions as you learn.

At the Discovery stage, focus on clarity and priorities rather than detailed timelines.

docs.title: Now, next, later roadmap
docs.text:
A Now, Next, Later roadmap is a simple way to organize your priorities without committing to specific delivery dates.

It separates your work into three categories:

  • Now: The most important problem or opportunity you're currently investigating.
  • Next: The problems or opportunities you expect to explore after your current priorities.
  • Later: Potential areas of focus that may become relevant as you learn more.

For example:

Now Next Later Understand why customers struggle to prepare weekly reports Explore ways to reduce manual data entry Investigate opportunities for advanced reporting Identify the information customers need most often Test possible approaches to organizing that information Explore integrations with additional systems

At this stage, your roadmap can include research activities, customer problems, and potential outcomes.

You don't need to assign exact dates to every item.

Review the roadmap regularly and move priorities as new evidence becomes available.

docs.title: Evidence-to-roadmap framework
docs.text:
Use this framework to turn your interview findings into potential roadmap priorities.

Start by reviewing your customer discovery and SME interview notes.

For each important finding, record:

  1. Customer insight: What did you learn?
  2. Problem or need: What underlying challenge does the insight reveal?
  3. Evidence: Which interviews, observations, or other sources support it?
  4. Desired outcome: What improvement would matter to the customer?
  5. Next step: What do you need to investigate, test, or clarify?

For example:

Customer insight Problem or need Desired outcome Next step Customers manually combine information from several spreadsheets Preparing reports requires significant time Reduce time spent preparing reports Investigate the reporting process in more detail Customers struggle to find important records Information is difficult to locate Make relevant information easier to access Explore how customers organize and retrieve records

This framework helps you maintain a connection between your research and the priorities you include in your roadmap.

docs.title: Opportunity-solution tree
docs.text:
An opportunity-solution tree is a visual framework for connecting a desired outcome to customer needs, potential solutions, and experiments.

It typically includes:

  • Desired outcome: The improvement you want to achieve.
  • Opportunities: Customer needs, problems, or pain points that could help you achieve the outcome.
  • Solutions: Possible approaches to addressing those opportunities.
  • Experiments: Ways to test assumptions about potential solutions.

At the Discovery stage, you can begin by identifying the desired outcome and mapping the customer opportunities you've uncovered.

You don't need to select or commit to solutions immediately.

As you move into the Validation stage, you can expand the tree to include possible solutions and experiments.

This approach can help you avoid becoming attached to one idea before exploring alternatives.

docs.title: Roadmap review
docs.text:
Your roadmap should change as your understanding of the customer improves.

When reviewing it, ask:

  • Are our priorities still supported by customer evidence?
  • Have we learned anything that changes the importance of a problem?
  • Are we focusing on customer outcomes or becoming attached to specific features?
  • What assumptions remain untested?
  • What should we investigate next?
  • Are there opportunities we should remove or postpone?

Record significant changes and the reasons behind them.

This helps you understand how your product direction evolves and communicate those decisions to your team, advisors, or other stakeholders.

docs.title: Miro
docs.text:
Miro is a collaborative digital whiteboard that can help you organize customer insights, visualize priorities, and build product roadmaps.

You can use it to:

  • Group findings from customer discovery and SME interviews
  • Identify recurring problems and themes
  • Create a Now, Next, Later roadmap
  • Map customer opportunities and possible solutions
  • Collaborate with team members and advisors

Start with a simple board rather than building a complicated planning system.

For example, create one area for interview findings, another for customer problems, and a third for your roadmap priorities.

This allows you to connect the evidence you've collected to the decisions you're making.

Review Miro's available templates, features, and sharing settings to choose an approach that fits your needs.
